To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mice lacking AlkB in NCCs have cleft palate and hypoplastic mandible.
mice lacking BMP type-I receptor Alk2 (ALK2) in the neural crest show craniofacial malformations including cleft palate.
mice lacking Alks2 in the neural creast display multiple craniofascial defects including clet palate and a hypotropic mandible.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that govern the development of the neural crest and its derivatives, and the signaling molecules that regulate this process.
the role of BMP type I receptors in craniofacial development.
the identification and characterization of the genes and molecular mechanisms that regulate the migration, differentiation and survival of neural crest cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
BMP signaling via Alk receptors regulates the formation and/or maintenance of neural crest derived craniofacial cartilage.
the Alk2 receptor has a non-redundent and essential role in craniofacial development.
BMP signaling through Alk2 is required for normal formation of a subset of neural crest derived structures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the craniofacial phenotype observed in the Alk2 mutant is due to a failure of neural crest cells to differentiate into the correct craniofacial cell types.
Alk2 is a critical regulator of neural crest development and function.
Alk2 is required for normal craniofacial morphogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Alk2 signaling is required for normal development of the palate and the mandible.
Alk2 is required for normal development of the craniofacial skeleton.
the Alk2 receptor plays an essential role in the formation of the craniofacial complex.
